Question: Rachel and Robert run on a circular track. Rachel runs counterclockwise and completes a lap every \(90\) seconds, and Robert runs clockwise and completes a lap every \(80\) seconds. Both start from the start line at the same time. At some random time between \(10\) minutes and \(11\) minutes after they begin to run, a photographer standing inside the track takes a picture that shows one-fourth of the track, centered on the starting line. What is the probability that both Rachel and Robert are in the picture?
Solution:
Assume the runners maintain constant speeds and that the photograph time is chosen uniformly over the whole stated minute. Let \(t\) be the number of seconds since they started, so \(600\le t\le660\).

The photographed quarter of the track extends one-eighth of a lap on each side of the starting line. A runner is therefore visible from one-eighth of a lap before each return to the start until one-eighth of a lap afterward. The symmetry of this arc makes the runners' opposite directions irrelevant to these time windows.

Rachel returns to the start at \(t=630\). One-eighth of her lap takes \(90/8=11.25\) seconds, so her visibility window is
\[
[618.75,641.25].
\]
Her neighboring returns at \(540\) and \(720\) have visibility windows entirely outside the stated minute, so this is her only relevant window.

Robert returns at \(t=640\), and one-eighth of his lap takes \(80/8=10\) seconds. His relevant window is
\[
[630,650].
\]
His neighboring returns at \(560\) and \(720\) likewise contribute no other window in the minute.

Both runners are visible precisely during the overlap \([630,641.25]\), lasting \(11.25\) seconds. Under uniform sampling, endpoints do not affect the probability, and
\[
P=\frac{11.25}{60}=\boxed{\frac{3}{16}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

Without the uniform-time assumption, no unique probability follows. For example, choosing the time uniformly between \(600\) and \(610\) seconds gives probability \(0\), whereas choosing it uniformly between \(635\) and \(640\) seconds gives probability \(1\). Thus \(3/16\), choice C, is conditional on uniform sampling over the whole minute.
